criteria.descriptor: Rollout mechanics and monitoring signals are technically correct: shadow vs canary are used accurately, operational metrics (latency percentiles, throughput, GPU/cost, error rate) are real and correctly categorized, and quality signals (LLM-as-judge / labeled samples, schema validity, refusal/hallucination rate, catastrophic forgetting, drift) are described accurately. No invented mechanisms or false claims (e.g., treating uptime as a quality signal, or claiming the offline win guarantees production quality).

Covers both asks: a progressive rollout plan with a rollback/version-pinning safety net, AND two distinct monitoring categories (operational vs output-quality) each with concrete signals, plus the regression/drift and live-feedback dimension. Full marks require both the rollout and the operational-vs-quality split; partial credit if one category or the rollback plan is thin or missing.

Justifies the choices: why progressive rollout beats a hard swap (limits blast radius, enables comparison), and specifically why quality monitoring for an adapted LLM needs more than uptime dashboards (no cheap ground-truth signal; 'up and fast' can still be 'worse'). Trade-offs such as merged vs unmerged adapter serving, or offline-vs-live evaluation gap, strengthen the score.

Answer is well-organized and uses correct vocabulary (shadow/canary/champion-challenger, p95, LoRA adapter, LLM-as-judge, drift, catastrophic forgetting). The operational and quality signal lists are clearly separated and easy for a reviewer to tick off; reasoning is stated concisely rather than as an undifferentiated list.

expected_answer_points: Rejects a hard cutover in favor of progressive rollout -- shadow deployment and/or a canary that routes a small traffic percentage and ramps up gradually while keeping the current model as champion for comparison
Includes a safety net: version-pin the base model and adapter, define acceptance thresholds from the offline eval, and keep an automated rollback / kill switch tied to alerts

Names concrete operational/system signals: latency percentiles (p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec), error/timeout rate, GPU memory/utilization, and cost per request (optionally noting unmerged-adapter serving overhead)

Names concrete output-quality signals: task quality via labeled/human-reviewed samples or LLM-as-judge, output format/schema validity, refusal/hallucination rate, and output length/tone distribution vs the previous model
Flags capability regression / catastrophic forgetting from fine-tuning and/or input drift over time, arguing quality evaluation must be continuous rather than a one-time pre-launch gate
Incorporates live feedback signals -- human spot-checks, thumbs up/down, or a downstream business KPI (escalation/edit/resolution rate) -- because offline eval cannot capture the live distribution

Explains why quality monitoring is special: LLM output has no cheap ground-truth correctness signal, so a service can be fully 'up' and fast yet silently degrade, requiring semantic metrics plus human-in-the-loop
common_pitfalls: Treats the adapted model like an ordinary microservice -- lists only uptime, latency, and error rate and never addresses output quality, which is the crux of the question
Proposes a direct hard swap (or a manual all-at-once deploy) with no shadow/canary stage and no rollback or kill switch
Assumes the offline eval win guarantees production quality, so no live evaluation, canary sampling, or feedback loop is proposed
Ignores capability regression / catastrophic forgetting -- assumes the LoRA adapter can only add skill and never degrade general behavior
Omits version pinning of the base model and adapter, leaving no way to reliably reproduce or revert to a known-good state
Over-scopes the answer into a full retraining/RLHF or A/B statistical-significance pipeline instead of the requested deployment-and-monitoring plan
reference_answer:
Don't hard-swap; roll out progressively.

First shadow-deploy: mirror a copy of live traffic to the adapted model without returning its answers to users, and diff its outputs against the current model on real inputs. Then canary: route a small slice (e.g. 5%) of real traffic to the adapted model while the current model stays the 'champion', and ramp 5% -> 25% -> 100% only while metrics stay healthy. Pin the exact base-model and adapter versions and keep a one-click rollback / kill switch wired to alert thresholds, so a regression reverts in minutes.

Operational/system signals: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec, requests/sec), error and timeout rate, GPU memory and utilization, and cost per request. Serving the LoRA adapter unmerged adds a little per-request overhead; merging the weights removes it at the cost of multi-adapter flexibility.

Output-quality signals: task quality on a stream of labeled or human-reviewed canary samples (or an LLM-as-judge), output format/schema validity, refusal and hallucination rate, and output length/tone distribution versus the champion. Also watch for capability regression -- fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting on general tasks -- and for drift as the input mix shifts, so quality evaluation must be ongoing, not a one-time gate. Feed in human spot-checks, thumbs up/down, and a downstream KPI such as escalation or human-edit rate.

Quality monitoring needs more than uptime dashboards because an LLM has no cheap ground-truth correctness signal: the service can be 100% 'up' and fast while silently producing worse replies. You only catch that with semantic/quality metrics and human-in-the-loop review, not HTTP 200s.
